**Surah al-Bayyinah**

It is also called Surat al-Qiyamah, Surat al-Balad, Surat al-Munfakkin, Surat al-Bariyyah, and Surat Lam Yakun. Al-Bahr (*al-Bahr al-Muhit*) says: "It is Meccan according to the majority." Ibn al-Zubayr and ʿAta' ibn Yasar said: "It is Medinan." Ibn ʿAtiyyah reported this. In *Kitab al-Tahrir*, it is Medinan, and this is the view of the majority. Abu Salih narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that it is Meccan, and Yahya ibn Salam preferred this view. End of quotation. Ibn al-Faras said: "The more well-known view is that it is Meccan." Ibn Mardawayh narrated this from ʿAʾishah (may Allah be pleased with her). Ibn Kathir, however, asserted that it is Medinan, and he cited as evidence what Imam Ahmad, Ibn Qani' in *Mu'jam al-Sahabah*, al-Tabarani, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Khaythamah al-Badri, who said: "When the verse ﴿Those who disbelieved among the People of the Book and the polytheists were not going to desist...﴾ was revealed, down to its end, Jibril (peace be upon him) said: 'O Messenger of Allah, your Lord commands you to recite it to Ubayy.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said to Ubayy (may Allah be pleased with him): 'Jibril (peace be upon him) commanded me to recite this surah to you.' Ubayy said: 'Was I mentioned there, O Messenger of Allah?' He said: 'Yes.' Then he wept."

This is the more correct view. Its number of verses is nine according to the Basran reckoning and eight according to others.

Regarding its virtue, there is what Abu Musa al-Madini narrated in *al-Ma'rifah* from Isma'il ibn Abi Hakim, from Matar al-Muzani or al-Madani, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Allah, the Exalted, hears the recitation of ﴿Those who disbelieved...﴾ and says: 'Rejoice, My servant. By My might, I will not ask you about any of the states of this world or the Hereafter, and I will surely grant you a place in Paradise until you are pleased.'"

As for its connection to what precedes it: His saying, the Exalted, in it, ﴿Those who disbelieved...﴾ and so on, serves almost as a justification for the sending down of the Qur'an, as if it were said: "We have sent it down, because those who disbelieved were not going to desist from their disbelief until a Messenger came to them, reciting purified scriptures, and that is this revealed book. So do not be heedless."

**In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful.**

﴿Those who disbelieved among the People of the Book﴾, that is, the Jews and the Christians. Their being referred to by this title is said to be for the sake of emphasizing the enormity of their disbelief. It is also said that it indicates the cause of what is attributed to them regarding the promise to follow the truth, since the basis of that is their finding it in their scripture. This rests on a matter that will come, God willing, in the verse later on.

Using the relative clause as a verb (*kafaru*) indicates that their disbelief occurred after their prophets (peace be upon them) through the individual pieces of knowledge regarding the attributes of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. The particle *min* (from) is partitive, as the great guide of guidance, Shaykh Abu Mansur al-Maturidi, said in *al-Ta'wilat*, and not explanatory, because among them were those who did not disbelieve after their prophet and remained upon the correct belief until Allah caused them to die. He counted among these the Melkites from among the Christians, and it was said that they were upon the truth before the mission of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). An explanatory *min* would require that all of them disbelieved before the mission, but the apparent meaning contradicts this. The partitive reading has been supported by what is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with both of them) that the intended People of the Book were the Jews who lived on the outskirts of Medina, from the tribes of Banu Qurayzah, al-Nadir, and Banu Qaynuqa. Some said: "We do not concede that an explanatory *min* requires that all of them disbelieved before the mission, since it is possible that the designation of them as ‘those who disbelieved’ is in view of their condition after the mission, as if it were said: 'These disbelievers did not desist,' and they were specified as the People of the Book."

﴿And the polytheists﴾: these are those who held that Allah, glorified be He, had a partner, whether an idol or something else. Some restricted them to the worshippers of idols, because the polytheists of the Arabs in Mecca, Medina, and their surroundings were like this, and they are the ones intended here, according to what is narrated from the scholar (Ibn ʿAbbas). Whatever the case, the conjunction is over the People of the Book. It does not follow, on the partitive reading, that none of them were disbelievers, which would necessitate shifting to the explanatory reading, because they are a part of the whole, as some eminent scholars have stated. The possibility that the polytheists are meant as the People of the Book and their polytheism is their saying, "The Messiah is the son of Allah," and "ʿUzayr is the son of Allah," Allah is exalted far above that, is not valid. The conjunction is for the difference in the designation, which is nothing. It was also read as *wal-mushrikun* (and the polytheists) in the nominative, as a conjunction over the relative pronoun. Interpreting the common reading as that, and considering that the genitive is by proximity, is of questionable status.

The prepositional phrase in the position of a circumstantial clause refers to the pronoun in *kafaru*. His saying, the Exalted, ﴿desisting﴾ is the predicate of *yakun* (was). *Infikak* originally means the separation of things that were joined with some kind of detachment, and it is intended here to mean departing from what they were upon, which you will come to know, God willing. So the adjective is an active participle from *infakka* in its complete sense, not the incomplete one that enters upon a subject and predicate. Some grammarians claimed that it is an adjective of that (the incomplete verb), with a deleted predicate, meaning "promising to follow the truth" or something similar. This was criticized, apart from it being contrary to the apparent meaning, on the grounds that the predicate of *kana* and its sisters may not be deleted in ordinary usage, nor in the sense of "only," and not when there is no particle of protection; that is, in this world, necessarily.

His saying, the Exalted, ﴿until there comes to them the clear evidence﴾ is related to *munfakkin*. *Al-bayyinah* is an adjective in the sense of the active participle, meaning the one that makes the truth clear, or it is in its well-known meaning, which is the proof that establishes the claim. It may mean the miracle, and this applies to both interpretations.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 98, verses 2–3:

Then His saying, ﴿a Messenger﴾, is a substitute (badal kull min kull, "substitution of the whole for the whole") for it, or it is the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject, meaning: it is a Messenger. Its tanwin (the nunation on the noun) is for magnification (tafkhim), and what is meant by it is our Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. His, glorified is He, saying, ﴿from Allah﴾, in the position of a qualifier (sifah) for it, conveys relational magnificence (al-fakhamah al-idafiyyah), so it confirms what the tanwin conveyed of intrinsic magnificence (al-fakhamah al-dhatiyyah). His, exalted is He, saying, ﴿reciting purified pages﴾, is another qualifier for it, or a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in its first qualifier, just as His, glorified is He, saying, ﴿therein are upright scriptures﴾, is a second qualifier for ﴿pages﴾, or a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in its first qualifier, namely ﴿purified﴾. It is also permissible that the qualifier or circumstantial clause here be only the prepositional phrase, and that ﴿scriptures﴾ be in the nominative as the agent (fa'il). Applying the term "clear proof" (bayyinah) to him, upon him be blessings and peace, is evident according to the first meaning. According to the last meaning, it is by considering that his character and qualities, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, reached the limit of being miraculous, as al-Ghazali said in al-Munqidh min al-Dalal. Al-Busiri alluded to this with his saying:

"Let it suffice you, as a miracle among the unlettered, that you had knowledge in the age of ignorance, and the discipline you received in orphanhood."

From this one learns the wisdom in his, upon him be blessings and peace, being made an orphan. Or it is by considering the multiplicity of his miracles, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, other than what has been mentioned, and their manifestation.

It is also permitted that by "clear proof" is meant the Qur'an, since it makes the truth clear, or since it is a miracle that establishes the claim. This was narrated from Qatadah and Ibn Zayd. And ﴿a Messenger﴾ (rasul), it has been said, is a badal ishtimal (substitution of inclusion, "substitution by containment") or also a badal kull min kull, with an omitted noun, meaning: a clear proof, or a revelation, or a miracle, or the book of a Messenger. Or it is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: it is a Messenger, and an omitted noun is understood with it, as you have heard. It is also permitted that ﴿a Messenger﴾ be the subject, described by what follows, and its predicate the clause ﴿reciting﴾, etc. The subject and its predicate together explain the "clear proof." It has also been said that it is an interjected clause (i'tiradh) to praise it, and it has been said that it is a qualifier of it, with the Qur'an intended by it, and by the "purified pages" is meant the clear proof. The pronoun has been replaced by the noun, so it serves as the connecting link (rabit).

Ubayy and Abdullah (Ibn Mas'ud) read «rasulan» (a Messenger) in the accusative, as a circumstantial clause (hal) from "clear proof." The word ﴿pages﴾ (suhuf) is the plural of sahifah, and likewise al-sihaf are the parchments on which things are written. Its root meaning is "that which is spread out from a thing." By its purification is meant its being cleared of falsehood, by way of explicit metaphor (isti'arah musarrahah). It is also permitted that there be an implicit metaphor (isti'arah makniyyah) in the speech, or that the purification be of the one who touches them, by way of attributing the action figuratively (tajawwuz fi al-nisbah). It is as if it were said: pages that none touches except the purified. By ﴿scriptures﴾ (kutub) is meant written contents, and by ﴿upright﴾ (qayyimah) is meant straight, and their straightness is their speaking the truth.

In al-Taysir it is said: they are the books of the prophets, peace be upon them, and the Qur'an confirms them, so it is as though they are contained in it. His, upon him be blessings and peace, being described as reciting the aforementioned pages is based on the well-known view that he, upon him be blessings and peace, did not read or write, by way of figurative attribution to the object (tajawwuz fi al-nisbah ila al-maf'ul), because when he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, recited what was in them, it is as though he read them. It has been said that there is an omitted noun, meaning: like pages. It has been said that the "in" (fi) in ﴿therein﴾ refers to the pages, and there is an implicit metaphor by likening his, upon him be blessings and peace, recitation of the like of what is in them to the one who recites them. Or the "pages" is a metaphor for what is in them, by the relation of containment (`alaqat al-hulul). So in the pronoun of ﴿therein﴾ there is istikhdam (using a word in one sense and returning a pronoun to it in another), since it returns to "pages" in its literal meaning.

It has been said: by the Messenger is meant Gabriel, peace be upon him, and by the pages are meant the pages of the angels, peace be upon them, copied from the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz), and by their purification is meant what has preceded. The meaning of his, upon him be blessings and peace, reciting them is evident, but making it a metaphor for his receiving revelation of them is not appropriate. The more preferable view is to take "the Messenger" as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and this is what was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, Muqatil, and others.

The scholars have differed greatly about the meaning intended by the verse, to the extent that al-Wahidi said in his book al-Basit that it is among the most difficult verses of the Qur'an in its composition and its interpretation. This is clarified on the basis that disbelief (kufr) is a description applying to each of the two groups before the mission, namely that the apparent meaning is: those who disbelieved from the two groups were not separated from what they were upon of disbelief until the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, came to them. And "until" (hatta) denotes the endpoint (intiha' al-ghayah), so it requires that they separated from their disbelief at the coming of the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and this contradicts the actual reality, and it is contradicted by

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 98, verse 4:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And those who were given the Book did not become divided except after the clear evidence had come to them﴾. This clearly indicates that their disbelief increased at that point. Jar Allah (al-Zamakhshari) said: The disbelievers of both groups used to say before the mission: "We will not cease from what we are upon of our religion until Allah, exalted is He, sends the promised Prophet, who is written in the Torah and the Gospel, and he is Muhammad, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him." Then Allah, exalted is He, related what they used to say. Then He, glorified is He, said: ﴿And they did not become divided﴾ etc., meaning: they used to consider that the unity of word and agreement upon the truth would occur when the Messenger came, but then what divided them from the truth and kept them upon disbelief was only his coming. The comparable example in speech is that a poor sinner says to one who admonishes him: "I will not cease from what I am upon until Allah grants me wealth." Then Allah, mighty and majestic is He, grants him that, and he increases in sinfulness. Then his admonisher says: "You were not ceased from sinfulness until you became wealthy, and you did not plunge your head into sin except after affluence," reminding him of what he used to say, as rebuke and censure. The summary of this is that the first is by way of relating their claim.

His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And they did not become divided﴾ etc. is a censure upon them. Allah, exalted is He, related their speech by way of rebuke and reproach, saying: "This is the outcome." Its apparent meaning is that He intended by their division from the truth that they were drawn into disbelief and falsehood, since the one entails the other. The mention of the polytheists is omitted in His saying ﴿And they did not become divided﴾ etc. because their state is known from the state of those who were given the Book, a fortiori. It has also been said, and it is close to that in one respect and clarifies it in another respect; that is: they were not ceased from what they were upon of the promise to follow the truth and to believe in the Messenger sent at the end of time, until there came to them what they had made an appointed time for gathering and agreement, so make it an appointed time for separation and division, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿And they did not become divided﴾ etc. In the expression ﴿ceased﴾ (munfakkin) there is an indication of the firmness of their promise.

It is well known among the People of the Book, to the point that they used to seek victory and say: "O Allah, grant us victory and help us through the Prophet sent at the end of time," and they would say to their enemies among the polytheists: "The time of a prophet has drawn near who will come confirming what we have said, and we will kill you along with him, a killing like that of 'Ad and Iram."

As for the polytheists, it probably occurred among their later generations after what was spread among the People of the Book and they believed its validity from what they witnessed, for example, from some trustworthy man among them from their people, such as Zayd ibn 'Amr ibn Nufayl, for he used to seek a prophet from the Arabs and say: "His time has drawn near, and he is from Quraysh, indeed from the Banu Hashim, indeed from the Banu 'Abd al-Muttalib." This is supported by the fact that before his mission, peace be upon him, more than one of them named his son Muhammad, hoping that he would be the awaited Prophet. And Allah knows best where He places His message. The expression of his coming in the present tense is in consideration of the state of the narrated situation, not in consideration of the state of the narration, as in His saying: ﴿And they followed what the devils recited﴾, meaning what they had recited.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they did not become divided﴾ etc. is a statement brought for further condemnation of the People of the Book in particular, by explaining that what was attributed to them of ceasing (from the promise) was not due to confusion in the matter, but after the truth had become clear, the situation had been made evident, and excuses had been entirely cut off. This is the secret behind describing them as those "given the Book," which indicates their complete capacity to study it and to comprehend what it contains of rulings and reports, among which is what concerns the Prophet, peace be upon him, and the validity of his mission, after their mention earlier by what functions as a collective noun for the two groups.

Since these and the polytheists, in consideration of their agreement upon the aforementioned opinion, are in the ruling of one group, what proceeded from them after the agreement was expressed, when announcing its occurrence through ceasing, and when explaining how it occurred through division, taking into account the independence of each of the two groups of the People of the Book, and as an indication that their ceasing from the aforementioned opinion was not by way of agreement upon another opinion, but by way of the old disagreement. The two explanations have been criticized on the grounds that there is nothing in the speech that indicates it is a narration except on the meaning of "not ceased from the promise to follow the truth." Al-Qadi 'Abd al-Jabbar said: The meaning is: those who disbelieved were not ceased from their disbelief even though the clear evidence came to them. Al-Imam criticized him, saying that interpreting the word "hatta" (until) in the manner mentioned is not from the language at all. Perhaps he meant that the intended purpose is the continuation of the negation, and that there is an ellipsis in the speech; that is: they were not ceased from their disbelief at any time until the time when the clear evidence came to them, except that he expressed it in the manner mentioned because it is more concise. There is also in it what is not hidden.

It has been said: The meaning is: they were not ceased from remembering the Messenger, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, with praises and virtues, until he came to them, and then they divided concerning him, and each of them said about him, peace be upon him, a false statement. This was criticized on the grounds that there is no indication that what was estimated as the object of ceasing is intended. It has been said: The meaning is: they were not ceased from their disbelief until the time of the coming of the Messenger, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him; then when he came to them, they divided: some of them believed and some of them persisted in their disbelief, and this suffices for acting upon the implication of "until."

It was criticized on the grounds that the apparent meaning of ﴿And they did not become divided﴾ etc. is a condemnation of all of them and a reproach against them, and His saying afterward supports this: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved among the People of the Book﴾ etc., and this is remote if division is taken to mean the belief of some and the persistence of others. It has been said: The meaning is: they were not ceased from their disbelief by being hesitant about it, but rather they were firmly resolved upon it, holding its truth as certain, until the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, came to them; at that point their thoughts and reflections were thrown into turmoil, and each doubted his religion and his doctrine. And there is in this what is not hidden.

It has been said: The meaning of ﴿munfakkin﴾ is "perishing," from their saying "infakka silā al-mar'a" (the two pubic bones of the woman separated) at childbirth, which is when they separate and do not rejoin. The meaning would be: they were not punished or perishing except after the proof had been established against them by the sending of messengers and the sending down of books. Close to this in meaning is what has been said: they were not ceased from life by dying and perishing until the clear evidence came to them, and this is, as you see, far-fetched. It has been said: The intended meaning is that they were not ceased from their religion in reality until the coming of the subsequent Messenger, who abrogates the scriptures that clarify its abrogation and invalidity; and when he came and that became clear, they ceased from it in reality, even if they remained upon it in form. There is in this what there is.

Abu Hayyan said: The apparent meaning is that the meaning is: they were not ceased, i.e., separated from one another, but rather each of them approved of the other's position upon what he had chosen for himself: this one from belief in his law, and that one from belief in his idols. The summary of this is that their affection was connected and their word was united until the clear evidence came to them.

﴿And those who were given the Book did not become divided﴾, i.e., among the polytheists, and some of them separated from others, so each said what indicates, in his view, the validity of his statement.

﴿except after the clear evidence had come to them﴾. It would have required, when it came, that they gather in following it. It is not hidden that his saying "rather each of them" etc. falls under the category of prohibition. Also, taking "And they did not become divided" as he took it is not apparent. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: Here there is an excellent meaning, which is that the intended sense is: these people were not ceased from the command of Allah, His power, and His regard, glorified is He, until He sends to them a warning Messenger through whom He, exalted is He, establishes the proof against them and completes the blessing upon whoever believes in him. It is as if He said: "They were not to be left neglected." There are similar instances of this in the Book of Allah, majestic is His majesty. This is what we have attained of question and answer, criticism and approval.

Then I say: What has preceded in establishing the difficulty is based on the view of those who hold the principle of the implication of the limit (mafhum al-ghayah), and they are the majority of jurists and a group of theologians, such as al-Qadi Abu Bakr, al-Qadi 'Abd al-Jabbar, Abu al-Husayn al-Basri and others, not the view of the others who oppose it, who are the companions of Imam Abu Hanifa and a group of jurists and theologians. Al-Amidi chose this and argued for it with what he argued, and refuted what opposes it from the evidences of the opponent. Upon this it is possible to say: Allah, glorified and exalted is He, first explained the state of those who disbelieved from both groups until the time of the coming of the Messenger, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, by His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿Those who disbelieved among the People of the Book and the polytheists were not ceased﴾, i.e., from the religion they were upon according to their belief in it, until the Messenger came to them. And since, according to that view, no mention was made of their state after the coming of the Messenger, peace be upon him, He explained it by His saying, majestic and exalted is He: ﴿And those who were given the Book did not become divided﴾ etc.; i.e., they did not become divided: so some of them recognized the truth and believed, and some others of them recognized it and were stubborn and did not believe at any time except after the clear evidence had come to them. He, glorified is He, omitted the mention of the state of the polytheists because He knew their state a fortiori. Then He, exalted is He, mentioned after the state of each of the two groups, the believer and the disbeliever, and what awaits each in the Hereafter, by His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved﴾ etc., and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who believed﴾ etc.

What I incline to among what has preceded is that the ceasing is from the promise to follow the truth, and perhaps the indication for taking this is contextual. It may admit another kind of interpretation, namely that the speech be placed under the category of "conflicting governors" (al-a'mal). It is said: "munfakkin" requires a complement, which is the thing ceased from, and "ta'tiyahum" (comes to them) requires a subject, and there is in the speech nothing but "the clear evidence," so each of them requires it. The verb "ta'tiyahum" was made to govern it, and the complement of "munfakkin" was omitted because it is indicated by it. It is as if it were said: "Those who disbelieved from both groups were not ceased from the clear evidence until the clear evidence came to them." Since the intended meaning of "the clear evidence" is the Messenger, the speech amounts to: "They were not ceased from the Messenger until he came to them." By non-ceasing from the Messenger, when he was not present at that time, is meant not ceasing from his remembrance and from the promise to follow him. The rest of the verse would then be according to what preceded, on the assumption that "munfakkin" means ceasing from the promise to follow the truth which they were upon. And if you wish, you may say regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they did not become divided﴾ etc., that it means: "And those who were given the Book did not become divided from the Messenger, nor did they cease from him by persisting in disbelief, except after he came to them." So reflect upon all that we have brought you, and Allah, exalted is He, knows best the secrets of His Book.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 98, verse 5:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they were not commanded except to worship Allah﴾ is a circumstantial clause (jumlah haliyyah) conveying the extreme ugliness of what they did. The meaning of "command" (al-amr) here is taklif (religious obligation) in general, and its object (muta'alliq) is omitted. The lam is for causation (ta'lil). The discussion of the causes of God's actions (ta'lil af'alihi) is well known. The exception (istithna') is an incomplete exception (mufarragh) from the most general category of causes; that is: "and the situation is that they were not charged in their Scripture with what they were charged with for any reason except for the sake of worshipping Allah, exalted is He."

Al-Farra' said: The Arabs put the lam in the place of "an" (that) with commands, as in "we were commanded that we might submit" (li-nuslima), and likewise with desire, as in ﴿Allah desires to make clear to you﴾. So here it has the meaning of "an"; that is: "except that they worship Allah." This is supported by the reading of Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud): "except that they worship Allah" (illa an ya'budu Allah), so that the worship of Allah exalted is what is commanded, and the command is on its literal sense. The first (view) is the more apparent, and on it 'Alam al-Huda Abu Mansur al-Maturidi said: From this verse is known the meaning of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And I did not create the jinn and humankind except that they should worship Me﴾, that is, except by commanding them to worship, so that the obedient is distinguished from the disobedient. This, as al-Shihab said, is a good and subtle statement.

﴿Sincere in their religion for Him﴾ means: making their religion purely for Allah, exalted is He, so they associate nothing with Him, mighty and majestic is He. Thus "religion" is the object of "sincere" (mukhlisin). It is also permitted that it be in the accusative by dropping the preposition, and the object of "sincere" is omitted; that is: making themselves purely for Him, exalted is He, in religion. Al-Hasan recited "mukhlasin" with a fatha on the lam, and in that case this second possibility becomes specific, and the first is not possible. Indeed, it is also permitted that it be an accusative of the verbal noun (masdar), with the governing verb being "li-ya'budu," meaning: that they should acknowledge Allah, exalted is He, in worship, in religion.

﴿Upright (hunafa')﴾ means: inclining away from all deviant beliefs toward Islam, and in it is an emphasis on sincerity of the kind it contains. Thus al-hanaf means inclination toward uprightness, and the one who inclines toward crookedness is called ahnaf (bow-legged/inclined) out of optimism (tafa'ul), or it is a metonymy (majaz mursal) with two levels. From Ibn 'Abbas, the explanation of hunafa' here is "pilgrims (hujjaj)." From Qatadah, "circumcised (mukhtatinin), forbidding marriage with mothers and close relatives." From Abu Qilabah, "believing in all the messengers, peace be upon them." From Mujahid, "following the religion of Ibrahim, peace be upon him." From al-Rabi' ibn Anas, "facing the qiblah in prayer." From some, "gathering all of religion." The state of these sayings is not hidden.

﴿And establish the prayer and give the zakat﴾: if by these two is meant what is in their law of prayer and zakat, then the command to them is clear. If what is meant is what is in our law, then the meaning of their being commanded with them in their Scripture is that their being commanded to follow our law is a command to them with all its rulings, of which these two are part.

﴿That﴾ is a reference to what was mentioned: worship of Allah, exalted is He, with sincerity, establishing the prayer and giving the zakat; and the distancing demonstrative (dhalika), with what it contains of distance, is to indicate the loftiness of its rank and the elevation of its station in nobility.

﴿The upright religion (dinu al-qayyimah)﴾ means: the upright Scriptures (al-kutub al-qayyimah).

The definite article (alif-lam) is for prior reference (al-'ahd), pointing back to what was mentioned in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Therein are upright scriptures﴾. This is the view of Muhammad ibn al-Ash'ath al-Talaqani. Al-Zajjaj said: that is, the upright community (ummah qayyimah), i.e., the straight one. Many others said: that is, the upright creed (millah qayyimah), and the relative distinction between religion (din) and creed (millah) validates the construction. Some did not supply a noun being qualified, and took "qayyimah" to mean creed. It was also said: that is, the upright proofs (hujaj qayyimah). 'Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud), may Allah be pleased with him, read: "al-dinu al-qayyimatu," and it was said the feminine form is by interpreting din as millah, and it was said the ha' is for emphasis (mubalaghah).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 98, verse 6:

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved among the People of the Book and the polytheists will be in the fire of Hell.﴾ It has been said: this is a statement of the condition of the two groups in the Hereafter after the statement of their condition in this world. The polytheists are mentioned so that it would not be thought that the ruling is restricted to the People of the Book, in accordance with the restriction of witnessing the signs of prophethood in the Book to them. Thus, by "those who disbelieved" are meant those mentioned at the beginning of the surah. There is a possibility in this which we have pointed out, so do not overlook it.

The meaning of their being "in the fire of Hell" is that they will arrive at it on the Day of Resurrection, but since this is certain, it has not been stated explicitly. The sentence is nominal, or the complement of the preposition is understood in the sense of the future, or they are in it now, using the name of the fire of Hell for what necessitates it, which is disbelief, as a metonymy (majaz mursal) by naming the cause by its effect. A metaphor has also been permitted. It has been said: what they are in of disbelief and sins is itself the fire, except that it has appeared in this worldly existence in an accidental form, and in the next existence they will shed it and it will appear in its real form. A parallel of this has passed more than once.

﴿Abiding therein forever﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in the predicate. The sharing of the two groups in entering the fire by way of eternal abiding does not preclude the difference in their punishment in manner, for Hell, may God protect us, has levels (darakat), and its punishments are of various kinds. So the People of the Book are punished at one level of it with one type of punishment, and the polytheists at a lower level with a harsher punishment, because their disbelief is more severe than the disbelief of the People of the Book. The People of the Book disbelieved in the Messenger of God, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, while knowing his noble attributes and the soundness of his mission from their own Book, whereas the polytheists had no such knowledge. This knowledge does not necessitate that their punishment be harsher than the punishment of the polytheists, nor equal to it, for polytheism is a great wrong. Additionally, there were joined to it kinds of disbelief among the polytheists which the People of the Book do not have. The verse has been cited as evidence for the eternal abiding of disbelievers in the Fire absolutely.

﴿Those﴾ is a demonstrative referring to them in view of their being characterized by the vile traits mentioned, and the sense of distance in it is due to the distance of their station in evil; that is, "those distant ones mentioned" ﴿are the worst of creation﴾, i.e., of created beings. It has been said: i.e., of mankind. The meaning has been said to be: they are the worst of creation in deeds, so the sentence is in the position of a reason for their eternal abiding in the Fire. It has been said: the worst of them in station and destination, so it would be an emphasis on the awfulness of their condition. The first has been preferred, since it accords with what will come, God willing, concerning the believers. In any case, the generality, as it has been said, is problematic, for Iblis and his hosts are worse than them in deeds and station, and likewise the polytheists and hypocrites, insofar as they combined hypocrisy with polytheism, and He, glorified is He, has said: ﴿Indeed, the hypocrites will be in the lowest level of the Fire﴾. Some have said: it is not far-fetched that among the disbelieving nations there are those worse than them, such as Pharaoh and the slayer of the she-camel. It has been answered that by "creation" are meant their contemporaries, but it is still not free of the problem with Iblis and the like. It has been answered that this is when the restriction is real, but when it is relative to the believers according to their own claim, there is no problem; for the meaning becomes: those are the worst of creation and not others among the believers, as they claim, in outcome or in condition. It has been said: by "creation" is meant mankind. By their being the worst is meant their being worst in terms of deeds, and it is not far-fetched that according to this they are the worst of all creation, because their disbelief, together with knowledge of the soundness of his prophethood, peace be upon him, and witnessing his miracles both intrinsic and extrinsic, and the promise of faith in him, peace be upon him, and with their introducing doubt into the hearts of those who come after them, and their causing the misguidance of many people, and other vices comprised and implied by it, constitutes the worst and most abominable disbelief, the like of which is not possible for anyone of mankind until the Day of Resurrection. Likewise all their other deeds: altering words from their places, turning people away from him, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, and fighting him, peace be upon him. That the disbelief of Pharaoh and the slayer of the she-camel and their acts are in that degree is not accepted. And it is necessary to hold that the hypocrites enter the generality of "those who disbelieved," or that their disbelief and deeds are below the disbelief and deeds of those mentioned. There is something in this which is not hidden, so consider it.

It has been said: the intended "those who disbelieved" are not specific peoples who were spoken of first, but rather the more general category including them and others from the remote past to its end. This, however, as it stands, is not complete without taking "creation" to mean mankind, so do not overlook it.

Al-A'raj, Ibn 'Amir and Nafi' read "al-bari'a" here and in what follows with a hamza. It has been said: this is the original, from baraa'ahum Allah, meaning He originated and created them, so it is fa'ila in the sense of maf'ula. However, the general body of the Arabs, except the people of Makkah, committed to easing the hamza by substitution and assimilation, and so they said "al-bariyya," as they said "adh-dhurriyya" and "al-khabiyya." It has been said: it is not the original; rather "al-bariyya" without hamza is from al-bara (the earth), meaning dust, so it is a root in its own right, and the two readings differ in origin and root, and agree in meaning in one opinion, namely that the intended meaning in both is mankind, and differ in it also in another opinion, namely that the intended by the hamzated form is the vicegerent, encompassing angels and jinn as well as humans, and by the unhamzated form the human beings created from dust alone. In any case, the reading with hamza is not an error, how could it be, since it has been transmitted from one whose infallibility is established, and since hamza is the dialect of the people to whom the Book was revealed, may God's blessings and peace be upon him.

Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds: this is a description of the good states of the believers, following the description of the bad state of the disbelievers, in keeping with the Qur'anic pattern (*sunnah*, established practice) of pairing warning (*tarhib*) with promise (*targhib*). Or it follows what we indicated earlier.

Isam al-Din said: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve﴾ and so on, is like an emphasis on His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and that is the upright religion﴾, since there is no affirmation that it is the upright religion beyond that the recompense of the one who turns away is this, and the recompense of the one who complies is that. However, that required His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, those who believe﴾ and so on. It seems that it was separated to give the impression of a lack of connection between the two sentences, though not in the subject nor in the predicate.

﴿Those﴾, that is, those described by what is the furthest extent of nobility and excellence, through faith and obedience.

﴿They are the best of creation.﴾ Ḥumayd and ʿĀmir ibn ʿAbd al-Wāḥid read: "they are the best (*khiyār*) of creation." This is the plural of *khayr*, like *jiyād* and *jīd*.

﴿Their reward﴾ in return for what they had of faith and acts of obedience, ﴿with their Lord are Gardens of Eden beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever﴾. Its parallels have already been mentioned. In the mention of their praise as "the best of creation" and the mention of the reward, which indicates that what they were granted is in return for what they were described with, and clarifies that it is from Him, may He be exalted, and in the reference to the title of Lordship (rubbubiyyah), which indicates nurturing and bringing to perfection, along with its attribution to their pronoun, the plural of "gardens," restricting them by their attribution and by what increases their delight, and the emphasis of abiding forever by "forever," there is an indication of the utmost goodness of their condition, which is not hidden.

Apparently the sentence ﴿they are the best of creation﴾ is the predicate of the demonstrative noun, and so is what follows it. Some eminent scholars claimed that what is more fitting with the preceding parallel structure is to make it a parenthetical clause (i'tirad), with the predicate being what follows it, but this requires consideration. The words of the Exalted: ﴿God is pleased with them﴾ form a grammatical resumption (isti'naf) and an announcement of what He, Mighty and Majestic, has graciously bestowed beyond what was mentioned of the recompense for their deeds. It may also be explanatory (bayani), an answer to one who says: "Do they have anything beyond that?" It has also been permitted that it be a predicate following a predicate, or a circumstantial clause (hal) with "qad" (indeed) assumed or not assumed. It has also been permitted that it be a supplication for them from their Lord, which is a metaphor for bestowing existence along with an increase in honor, but this is contrary to the apparent meaning, and the conjunction of His words ﴿and they are pleased with Him﴾ to it makes it remote. Their being pleased is explained by the fact that they have attained the furthest of desires and the highest of aims, and there has been made available to them what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and what has not occurred to the heart of any human.

﴿That﴾, i.e., what He mentioned of the reward and the good pleasure, ﴿is for him who fears his Lord﴾. For fear (khashyah) is the foundation of true happiness and of attaining the lofty ranks; for without it, prohibitions and sins would not be abandoned, and one would not prepare for a Day on which people will be seized by their forelocks and feet. In this is an indication that mere faith and righteous deeds do not lead to the highest ranks and to a greater good pleasure from God; rather, what leads to it is the fear of God, the Exalted, and ﴿Only those among His servants who have knowledge fear God﴾. For this reason al-Junayd, may his secret be sanctified, said: "Contentment is in proportion to the strength of knowledge and firmness in gnosis (ma'rifah)." 'Isam al-Din said: "The most apparent view is that this refers to what the reward and good pleasure are consequent upon, namely faith and righteous deeds." This was criticized on the grounds that it contains heedlessness of what was mentioned, and that then there would be no great benefit in His words ﴿That...﴾ etc. The mention of the title of Lordship, which indicates ownership and nurturing, is to signal the reason for fear and to warn against being deceived by the nurturing.

The words of the Exalted ﴿Indeed, those who believe...﴾ etc. have been cited as evidence that humans are superior to angels, since it is clear that by "those who believe" is meant believing humans. There are narrations that indicate this.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu Hurayrah, traced to the Prophet: "Do you marvel at the station of the angels with God? By Him in whose hand is my soul, the station of the believing servant with God on the Day of Resurrection is greater than the station of the angel. Recite, if you wish: ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds—they are the best of creation﴾."

Ibn Mardawayh related from A'ishah, who said: "I said: O Messenger of God, who is the most honored of creation before God?" He said: "O A'ishah, do you not recite: ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds—they are the best of creation﴾?"

You know that this is apparent in that by "al-bariyyah" (creation) is meant creation in general, so that the argument is complete. Then it also requires including the prophets, peace be upon them, in the generality of "those who believe and do righteous deeds," by not intending by them a specific people; for if they were not included, it would follow that the common humans, i.e., those among them who are not prophets, are preferred over the elite of the angels, namely their messengers, peace be upon them. That is something none of the people of the Sunnah has held, rather they declare disbelief (takfir) of whoever says it. So let this be noticed. The Imam (al-Razi) weakened the argument in his tafsir with what is not free from scrutiny. Perhaps the furthest from disputation (qil wa qal) is to make the restriction (hasr) relative to what the People of the Book and the polytheists claim, either verbally or in state, that they are the best of creation; and similarly the preceding restriction is made relative to what they claim, that the believers are the worst of creation. The soundness of what preceded in the narrations is open to objection. Then the apparent meaning of "those who believe" etc. is the counterpart of "those who disbelieve," and the more appropriate of those who are fair (ansafu) is what is within the relative clause, specifically. Some claimed that they are specific (persons).

Ibn Mardawayh related from Ali, may God honor his face, who said: "The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said to me: 'Did you not hear the words of God, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds—they are the best of creation﴾? They are you and your Shi'ah, and my appointment and your appointment is the Basin (al-hawd), when the nations come to the reckoning, they will be called radiant, with white marks (ghurran muhajjalin).'" The Imamiyyah related something similar from Yazid ibn Shurahil al-Ansari, scribe of the Commander (of the Faithful), may God honor his face.

In it is that he, peace be upon him, said this to him at the time of his death, with his noble head upon his chest, may God be pleased with him.

Ibn Mardawayh also related from Ibn Abbas, who said: "When this verse was revealed: ﴿Indeed, those who believe...﴾ etc., the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said to Ali, may God be pleased with him and honor his face: 'It is you and your Shi'ah on the Day of Resurrection, content and well-pleasing.'"

That is apparent in specification. Likewise is what al-Tabarsi, the Imamite, mentioned in Majma' al-Bayan from Muqatil ibn Sulayman, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn Abbas, that he said regarding the verse: "It was revealed concerning Ali, may God honor his face, and the people of his house." If its soundness is granted, there is no objection to it, since it does not require specification, but rather inclusion in the generality, and they are without doubt included in it by primary inclusion. As for what preceded, its soundness is not granted, for it entails that Ali, may God honor his face, would be better than the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace. The Imamiyyah, although they say that he, may God be pleased with him, is better than the prophets, even the Ulu al-'Azm (the prophets of steadfast resolve), peace be upon them, and better than the angels, even the closest (muqarrabun), peace be upon them, do not hold that he is better than the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace. If they say that the "best of creation" in that is restricted to all except him, peace and blessings be upon him, due to the proof indicating that he, may God bless him and grant him peace, is better than him, may God honor his face, it is said: it is also restricted to all except the prophets and angels, and those of the people of the Sunnah who hold that he is better, due to the proof indicating their superiority. In sum, there should be no doubt about the non-restriction of "those who believe and do righteous deeds" to the Commander (of the Faithful), may God honor his face, and his Shi'ah, nor to him, may God be pleased with him, and his household; and that, without establishing the soundness of those reports, is like plucking thorns with bare hands (kharta al-qatad). And God knows best.

Then, the reports that many verses of this surah have been abrogated are numerous. Among them, Imam Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, related from Ubayy that the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: "Indeed God commanded me to recite the Qur'an to you." Then he, peace be upon him, recited: ﴿Those who disbelieved among the People of the Book...﴾ and in it he recited: "If the son of Adam were to have a valley of wealth, he would seek a second; if he were given a second, he would seek a third; and nothing fills the belly of the son of Adam except dust; and God turns in mercy to whoever turns in repentance. Indeed, the religion with God is the ḥanīfiyyah, not polytheistic nor Jewish nor Christian; and whoever does that, it will not be rejected from him."

In some reports, the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, recited it thus: "Those who disbelieved among the People of the Book and the polytheists were not to be separated until there came to them the clear evidence: a messenger from God, reciting purified scriptures, in which are upright books. Indeed, the most upright religion is the ḥanīfiyyah, submitting, not polytheistic, nor Jewish, nor Christian. Whoever does righteous deeds, it will not be rejected from him. The People who were given the Book did not differ except after the clear evidence came to them. Indeed, those who disbelieved and barred from the way of God and abandoned the Book when it came to them—those are the worst of creation with God. The people were not but one nation; then God sent the prophets as bearers of good news and warners, commanding the people to establish prayer, give zakah, and worship God alone. Those are the best of creation with God; their reward with their Lord is Gardens of Eden beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. God is pleased with them and they are pleased with Him; that is for him who fears his Lord."

Ibn Mardawayh related this from Ubayy, may God be pleased with him, and it contradicts what is authentically reported from him, so it is not relied upon, as is not hidden from one acquainted with the science of hadith.
